reviews.reason: Binding an integer to an opaque PostgreSQL statement is private DB2 execution state; typed operations carry validated integer fields and bind them inside the owner process.
Binding a 64-bit value to a process-owned statement cannot cross the bus; bounded request fields are decoded and bound wholly inside DB2.
Statement text binding exposes an opaque handle and unbounded database plumbing; each wire operation validates bounded strings before DB2 performs its own bind.
Reading a double from an opaque result cursor is private row decoding; DB2 validates and encodes the domain value into a bounded typed reply.
Reading an integer from a process-owned result cursor cannot be remote API; complete operations decode rows and return explicit domain fields.
Reading a 64-bit column is local cursor traversal; DB2 owns the result lifetime and emits only the bounded typed domain value.
A borrowed text pointer into PostgreSQL result storage is process-local lifetime state; DB2 copies validated bounded text into operation replies before finalizing.
Transporting caller-supplied raw SQL would violate the DB2 ownership and schema boundary; every bus mutation names a declared operation with DB2-owned SQL.
Finalizing an opaque statement is local lifetime cleanup; DB2 releases all query resources before returning any operation reply.
Preparing caller-provided SQL and returning an opaque statement handle cannot cross a process boundary; declared operations prepare private fixed SQL inside DB2.
Incremental cursor stepping would create a chatty handle protocol; DB2 exhausts or bounds the result set and returns one complete structured reply.
Affected-row inspection belongs to the private statement lifetime; a mutation operation maps it to bounded domain evidence before replying.

canonical_index_code_search is index.code_search under another name: its whole body forwards to db2_code_index_code_search. Reviewed as the same operation rather than a second one, because a forward is not a boundary, and listed as a forward in the generator's table so it cannot quietly become a second implementation.

canonical_index_code_search_excluding_project is index.code_search_excluding_project under another name, forwarding to db2_code_index_code_search_excluding_project. It was the only caller of that backend, which is why the backend read as unconsumed while the search itself was in use. Reviewed as the same operation, and listed as a forward so the two cannot drift.

canonical_index_find is index.term_find_in_project with no project: its whole body calls canonical_index_find_project with a null one, which the statement then drops. Reviewed as the same operation, and listed as a forward so the two cannot drift.

The typed index.callers_find_scoped operation lists the recorded calls to a symbol, in one project or in all of them. The empty project is what separates it from index.callers_find beside it, which always names one. The two order differently as a result: this one leads with the project name when it is searching all of them, and with the path when it is not.

The typed index.callers_find_excluding_project operation lists the recorded calls to a symbol everywhere but one project. The exclusion is required -- an empty name is refused -- so it is not index.callers_find_scoped with a filter inverted, and naming a project to search and one to exclude at once is refused.

The typed index.term_find_excluding_project operation finds an identifier everywhere but one project. The exclusion is required -- an empty name is refused -- so this is not index.term_find_in_project with a filter inverted, and the two cannot be combined. The same three tiers apply, so a reply here may also be about a name the caller did not ask for.

The typed index.term_find_in_project operation finds an identifier within one project, or within all of them when the project is empty. The tiers are the same as index.term_find's -- exact, then prefix, then substring -- and with an empty project the two run the same statement, which is why one of them should eventually go. Its callers reach them separately today.
Installing the bounded fork/exec capture capability is private immutable process bootstrap; no callback pointer or command-execution surface crosses the event bus.

canonical_index_structure is index.file_definitions under another name. It used to run its own copy of the query without selecting line_end, leaving that member of every row it wrote uninitialised for its callers to read; it forwards now, so the two cannot drift again. Reviewed as the same operation rather than a second one, because a forward is not a boundary.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_bump operation increments an anti-pattern's hit count. It reports success whenever the statement ran, so bumping an identifier that does not exist looks exactly like bumping one that does. Recorded because the delete on the same table makes the opposite choice, and a caller using both would otherwise have to discover the difference.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_check operation reports which anti-patterns a path and command trip. No condition reaches the database: every anti-pattern is read, normalised and phrase-matched in the module, so the cost grows with the table on every call. The path and the command are joined into one string before matching, so a pattern can match across the join between them.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_delete operation removes an anti-pattern by identifier and reports an error when no row matched. That is the opposite of the bump beside it, which treats a missing row as success. Both choices are now on the record rather than being a difference nobody wrote down.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_exists_by_source_ref operation replaces the second duplicate check, which looks up the same table by the reference a pattern was drawn from rather than by its text. It is a separate operation rather than a flag on the first because the two answer differently for the same anti-pattern.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_exists_exact operation replaces the duplicate check. The match is exact: a pattern that differs by a character is a different pattern, which is what makes this usable as a duplicate guard and is worth stating because the wire cannot show it. A statement that could not run answers false, the same as an absent row.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_list operation lists every anti-pattern, most hit first and then most confident. Nothing limits the statement, so the wire's row bound is the only stop. The hit count is a running total the bump operation raises, so ordering by it ranks by how often something has been noticed rather than by how much it matters.

The typed learning.anti_pattern_list_hot operation lists the anti-patterns hit at least so often. Confidence does not enter the condition or the order, so a pattern hit many times and trusted by nobody is hot here and a rarely hit certainty is not. That is the backend's definition of hot, and it is only visible by reading the rows it returns.

The typed learning.artifact_citation_count operation replaces the citation count. It counts distinct sources, not citation rows, so an artifact cited twice by one source counts once -- a caller given a plain number cannot tell which was meant, so the policy says.

The typed learning.artifact_cite operation replaces the citation insert. The citing artifact is a foreign key and an unknown one is refused; the cited source is not checked at all, so a citation can name a source that does not exist. The span is written as zero to zero and is part of the key, so this records that a source was cited and never where in it, and a spanned citation added later would be a second row.

The typed learning.artifact_flag_review operation flags an artifact for review. It also sets the state back to proposed whatever the state was, so flagging a committed artifact un-commits it, which the name does not say. An empty reason is stored as the word flagged rather than refused. The payload merge happens in C rather than in SQL -- the json_build_object expression it replaced could never run against Postgres -- so an artifact that does not exist is refused rather than acknowledged.

Generates a random artifact identifier in the caller's buffer, touching no database. It stays private, and one property is worth recording while looking at it: when the platform random source fails the bytes are zeroed rather than the failure reported, so every caller in that state generates the same all-zero identifier.

The typed learning.artifact_link operation replaces the link insert. Both artifacts are foreign keys, so an unknown end is refused, but the kind is stored unchecked: a caller can record a relationship no reader understands, in a direction only it knows the meaning of. Linking the same pair and kind twice does nothing and is acknowledged.

The typed learning.artifact_register_exemplar operation replaces the exemplar insert. Unlike the queue inserts beside it, this one has no conflict clause, so registering the same artifact and collection twice fails rather than being ignored -- a difference worth recording because both look identical from the wire.

The typed learning.artifact_set_state operation replaces the state write. The statement stores whatever state it is given -- nothing checks the value against a set of legal states -- so a caller can put an artifact into a state no reader understands. That is the backend's behaviour and is on the record because the wire, which bounds only the length, cannot show it.

The typed learning.artifact_stamp_reflected operation replaces the reflection stamp. The time written is DB2's own clock and never crosses, so a caller can record that an artifact was reflected on but not when. An identifier naming nothing updates no row and is acknowledged the same as one that did, which the wire cannot show.

The typed learning.verdict_suppressed operation reports whether anything has been thumbed down under a tag and scope. Every failure path answers not suppressed: an empty tag, no connection, a statement that will not prepare. So the operation fails open, and a caller using it as a suppression gate lets suppressed content through whenever the database is unreachable. Recorded because a Boolean reply cannot say which of the two answers it is.

The typed learning.bandit_arms_list operation replaces the arm listing. What crosses is a JSON array of quoted arm identifiers built by hand: nothing escapes them, so an arm whose name contains a quote or a backslash produces a document the caller cannot parse, and an empty one is dropped. When the buffer fills the array is closed early, so a truncated listing is indistinguishable from a complete one. A read that fails returns the empty array it wrote before preparing the statement.

The typed learning.bandit_decision_close operation records the reward for a decision and closes it. The reward is stored as given -- nothing normalizes it, so what a bandit compares later is on whatever scale the caller chose -- and the closing stamp is DB2's clock. The statement is not checked to have matched a row, so closing a decision that does not exist, or one already closed, is acknowledged and overwrites the earlier reward.

The typed learning.bandit_decision_points operation lists the decision points that have been decided, newest first, stopping at 64. What crosses is a JSON array built by hand: nothing escapes the names, so one containing a quote or a backslash produces a document the caller cannot parse, and the array is closed early when the buffer fills. A truncated list, a list cut off at 64, and a complete one all look the same.

The typed learning.bandit_promotion_get operation replaces the promotion read. A decision point with no promoted arm reads back as the empty string, which is also what a promotion recorded as empty would look like; the operation has one result and cannot separate them. A caller treating empty as "no promotion" is right in practice and wrong in principle, which is worth saying once here.

The typed learning.bandit_promotion_set operation replaces the promotion write. There is one promotion per decision point, so setting a second replaces the first and the previous rollback arm is lost with it -- a caller wanting to keep it has to have read it first. The stamp is DB2's clock. An empty rollback arm is allowed, which records a promotion with nothing to fall back to.

Returning a raw calibration-profile JSON blob leaks storage and serialization across the boundary; a typed learning.calibration_threshold operation owns scoped fallback and profile interpretation in one request.

The typed learning.calibration_surfaces_with_data operation replaces the surface count. The threshold is inside the grouping rather than applied to the result, so it decides which groupings count as having data at all -- raising it does not filter a fixed set, it changes the set. Only events carrying a verdict are considered.
Parsing DB2-owned profile JSON is private operation logic; the future learning.calibration_threshold reply returns only the validated bounded threshold selected from the same scoped profile read.

Reorders a result set the caller already holds so local dependents sort first. It is presentation applied to memory the caller owns, issues no statement, and has nothing to do with the database once the results exist.

The typed index.callers_find operation lists the recorded calls to a symbol within a project. The callee is matched exactly, so an overload or a differently qualified name is a different symbol here. What it lists is what the extractor recorded, so a call it could not see -- through a pointer, a macro, a dynamic dispatch -- is absent rather than reported as unknown.

The typed index.code_search operation searches indexed file contents. An empty project searches every project rather than none. An empty query answers with nothing rather than failing, which is the one input that is not an error. Dotted paths and projects rooted under a dotted directory are excluded. The line is zero unless enrichment is asked for, and even then it is found by locating the snippet in the content, so it is a hint and can precede the real match.

The typed index.code_search_excluding_project operation searches every indexed project but one. The exclusion is required rather than optional -- the backend refuses an empty name -- so this is not index.code_search with a filter switched off, and the two cannot be combined: naming a project to search and a project to exclude in the same call is refused there. Everything else it does, including the enrichment hint, matches index.code_search.

The typed index.drift_candidates operation counts the projects index.requeue_drifted would enqueue. The two share one predicate in the backend, and the catalog records that so the pair cannot drift apart: a count that no longer matches what the requeue acts on would be worse than no count, because it would look like a preview.

The typed index.file_definitions operation lists the symbols defined in one file, in line order. Both the project and the file must be in the current generation, so a file indexed under an older one has no definitions here rather than an error. A line_end of zero means the extractor never recorded where the symbol ended, which reads the same as a symbol ending at line zero; the pair is only meaningful when line_end is at least line.

The typed index.project_count operation replaces the current-project tally used by the doctor surface. Only projects in the current lifecycle state are counted and that state is fixed policy, so a caller cannot include detached projects in the number.

The typed index.project_current_generation operation reads a project's current generation. It matches only a project in the current lifecycle state, so a retired project answers zero -- and so does one that never existed, and so does a read that failed, because the backend clears the output before doing anything. A caller cannot tell those apart, which matters because the generation is what the project-scoped deletes key on.

The typed index.project_delete operation deletes a whole indexed project. Aliases, generations and files all cascade off the projects row, so the reply's one deleted row stands for everything the project held. Unlike the file-index deletes beside it the name is not resolved through aliases, so naming an alias deletes nothing and reports zero -- the same reply as a project that was already gone.

The typed index.project_last_scan operation reads the newest scan stamp across every project in the current lifecycle state. The answer belongs to no project in particular -- one freshly scanned project makes the whole index look fresh. An empty stamp means no current project has ever been scanned, and is also what a failed read gives, since the buffer is cleared before the statement runs. The request carries nothing, because nothing the caller could say would narrow it.

The typed index.purge_files_matching operation replaces the file purge. The pattern is bound as a SQL LIKE pattern rather than a literal, so a caller sending a path containing a percent sign deletes more than it named -- and only the project's current generation is touched, so files from an older generation survive. Both are properties a deletion count cannot show.

The typed index.purge_hidden_pollution operation replaces the startup hygiene sweep that removes inadmissible hidden-path files from the current generation. Which paths are inadmissible, and the .gitmodules exemption that keeps legitimately indexed submodule declarations, are fixed policy: a caller cannot widen the deletion to reach files the ingest path admits.

The typed index.requeue_drifted operation replaces the maintenance enqueue that re-ingests projects whose files have drifted. The forced re-ingest, the status the new rows carry and the pending-or-running dedup are fixed policy: without the dedup a repeated sweep would pile duplicate work onto the ingest drain, and the operation could not claim safe idempotency.

The typed index.term_find operation finds where an identifier is defined or used, across every current project. It answers in tiers: exact first, then prefix, then substring, each only when the one before found nothing -- so a reply may be about a name the caller did not ask for, and nothing in it says which tier answered. Definitions sort before uses. Dotted paths and projects rooted under a dotted directory are excluded.

The typed index.unique_file_basename operation resolves a bare file name to a path. It answers only when exactly one file matches: two files with the same name give the empty answer, the same as no file at all, which is the point -- an ambiguous name must not resolve. The match is made in the module over every path in the project's current generation, so the cost is the whole file list on each call and no index helps.

The typed index.generation_abort operation replaces the abort. Only a pending generation is touched, so aborting one that is already visible does nothing -- which is the safety the condition exists for, and is invisible in an acknowledgement that looks the same either way.

The typed index.projection_generation_create operation opens a pending projection generation. It stamps the running build as both the extractor and the pipeline version, and over the bus that is the DB2 module's build, not the caller's -- the snapshot-diff route refuses to compare across extractor versions, so a module and daemon at different builds would make every generation incomparable with the ones before it. A project that is not current creates nothing and answers zero.

The typed index.generation_publish operation replaces the publish. It supersedes whatever the project had visible and makes this generation visible inside one transaction, which is the point: a reader never sees two visible generations, and never sees none. It is the only operation in this batch that holds a transaction, and that is why.

The typed index.generation_set_source_hash operation replaces the hash write. Unlike the abort beside it this statement has no condition on the generation's state, so the hash of a generation that is already visible can be changed after the fact -- which would make visible_source_hash report something the generation was not built from. That is the backend's behaviour and is recorded rather than fixed here.

The typed index.projection_generations_list operation lists a project's projection generations, newest first. Unlike the reads beside it nothing here is narrowed to what is current: pending, visible and superseded generations all appear, and the project is matched by name without asking whether it is still current. That is what makes it useful for telling a caller which generations it could have asked for.

The typed index.projection_edges operation lists a project's visible code projection edges. The structural weight is not a column: the module derives it from the relation name, so an unrecognised relation weighs one and a caller cannot tell that from a relation genuinely worth one. Only the visible generation of a current project is listed, so a project mid-projection has no edges here.

The typed index.projection_edges_for_generation operation lists one generation's edges by identifier. Unlike index.projection_edges beside it nothing here asks whether the generation is visible or the project current, which is what makes it usable for comparing two generations -- and what makes it able to return edges no reader should treat as the truth. The structural weight is derived from the relation name, not stored.

The typed index.project_fingerprint operation replaces the fingerprint read. The value is an md5 DB2 computes over the file paths and hashes of the project's current generation, so it is a summary of that generation rather than an identifier: it changes when the generation does, and comparing one project's fingerprint against another's is meaningless. A project with no files fingerprints the empty string rather than failing.

The typed index.projection_visible_id operation reads which projection generation is visible for a project. Both halves must be current: the generation must be visible and the project must be in the current lifecycle state, so a visible generation belonging to a retired project reads back as none. Zero is that answer, and also the answer for a project nobody has projected, and also what a failed read gives.

The typed index.visible_source_hash operation replaces the visible-generation read. Only a generation in the visible state is considered, so a project whose generations are all still pending reads back empty rather than reporting the newest one -- which is the behaviour a caller wants and cannot infer from an empty string alone.

The typed learning.collab_rule_approve operation replaces the approval. Only a rule still in the proposed state is touched, so approving one that was already rejected does nothing -- and unlike collab_rule_reject beside it, this backend does not report whether a row changed, so the caller cannot tell that from a successful approval. The two are otherwise identical statements, which is what makes the difference worth recording.

The typed learning.collab_rule_propose operation replaces the proposal insert. It returns the new rule's identifier, which is what the approve and reject operations need, and zero means the insert did not happen rather than naming a rule -- identifiers start at one. Nothing deduplicates, so proposing the same text twice creates two rules.

The typed learning.collab_rule_reject operation replaces the rejection. Its statement is the mirror of approve's, but its backend checks whether a row changed and reports that, so a caller can tell that the rule was not in the proposed state. The reply carries it rather than a bare acknowledgement, because throwing that away would make the two operations look alike when they are not.

The typed learning.collab_rule_retire operation replaces the retirement. It touches only an active rule, so a proposed one cannot be retired without being approved first -- the state machine is in the statement rather than anywhere a caller can see. Unlike most of the writes beside it the reply does distinguish: retiring a rule that was not active is refused, not acknowledged.
A PostgreSQL connection is private process state and cannot cross the bus; each caller is replaced by a bounded operation that owns its complete transaction inside DB2.

The typed maintenance.corpus_pipeline_stage_counts operation counts the corpus jobs in each stage and status. It groups over the jobs that exist, so a stage nothing has reached is missing from the reply rather than present with a count of zero -- a caller building a dashboard from this has to know the stages itself. The rows are ordered by stage then status, so the reply is stable between calls even though the counts are not.

The typed index.cross_repo_rebuild_build_deps operation replaces the pass that rebuilds cross-repo build dependencies from indexed manifests inside one transaction. Every filter is fixed policy: the manifest list, the vendored exclusion, the build-output subtrees, and the skip for self and external refs. The project cap is recorded too, because exceeding it makes tail repositories unmappable rather than merely slow.

The typed index.cross_repo_rebuild_identities operation replaces the pass that rebuilds project identities from indexed manifests inside one transaction. The manifest list and the vendored exclusion are fixed policy: a vendored manifest declares the vendored library's identity, not the host repository's, and claiming it would mis-resolve directives to the wrong repo.

The typed index.cross_repo_rebuild_routes operation replaces the pass that empties and rebuilds the cross-repo include route table inside one transaction. The routing heuristics are fixed policy and travel nowhere: quoted includes only, the fan-out threshold that suppresses ubiquitous headers, and the generated-build-header rejects. Each was tuned against live findings, and a caller able to send them could reroute a repository's symbol resolution.

The typed maintenance.css_migration_assert_conventions operation derives two facts about a project's CSS from its indexed rules. Two things the reply hides: it reads the style-graph and typed-fact configuration flags, which over the bus are the module process's flags and not the caller's, and answers zero when either is off -- the same zero as a project with nothing indexed. The timestamp is the caller's, not DB2's clock, so a caller with a wrong clock dates the facts wrongly.

The typed maintenance.css_migration_enumerate operation refreshes a project's CSS migration units from its component files. Two things the count does not show: it reads at most 4096 component files and stops, so a larger project reports 4096 and silently leaves the rest un-enumerated; and the upserts run one at a time with no transaction, so a failure part way leaves some units refreshed and reports failure for all of them. An existing unit keeps its state and its note; only the token counts are refreshed.

The typed maintenance.css_migration_rules_doc operation writes a conventions document derived from a project's indexed CSS. Most of it is a fixed template; three counts and a naming verdict come from the database, and a project with nothing indexed still gets the whole document with zeros in it, which reads as a specification rather than as an absence. The naming verdict is a heuristic on selector delimiters, not a fact anyone recorded.

The typed learning.curator_invalidate_doc operation stales the artifacts citing a document. It reads at most 1024 of the document's chunks and stops, so a larger document leaves the artifacts citing its later chunks valid and reports a count that looks complete. The invalidations run one chunk at a time with no transaction, so a partial run is reported as its partial count, and the invalidation event is written only when the count is above zero.

The typed maintenance.curator_reembed_all operation replaces the reset that returns committed artifacts to the proposed state after a curator version change. The kind list is the reason the policy is fixed rather than travelling: only those six kinds are re-derivable, and a caller able to send the list could demote artifacts that nothing will ever propose again, stranding them outside the committed set for good.

The typed maintenance.curator_reenqueue_extract_all operation replaces the pass that enqueues an extraction job for every current-generation document and re-arms the existing ones. Two properties are recorded rather than smoothed over: it runs three autocommitting statements with no surrounding transaction, so a reader can observe the state between them, and its number comes from a separate count query rather than the rows the mutations touched, so it is the queue afterwards and not the work done.

A pure string comparison against a fixed list of gap types; it issues no statement and reads no state. Crossing the bus to ask whether a word is in a list would be absurd, but the answer still has to agree on both sides: the list is shared vocabulary and belongs in a shared definition, not in a call. A caller that disagrees with DB2 about the canonical set writes gap types the queries never match.

The typed learning.curiosity_rescore_all operation replaces the pass that rescores open curiosity items. The weights decide what the system becomes curious about next, so a caller able to send them could steer its attention; they are fixed policy and travel as integer percents, since a float literal is not the same number on every reader. The pass also writes updated_at back to itself so a rescore does not read as an edit.

The same shape as the gap-type predicate beside it: a pure comparison against a fixed state list, no statement, no state read. Shared as a definition rather than as a call, for the same reason -- a caller with a different idea of the valid states stores rows the sweeps skip.

The typed maintenance.decision_log_list operation lists logged decisions by outcome, newest first. An empty outcome drops the condition rather than matching decisions whose outcome is unset, so the one filter a caller might most want -- decisions with no outcome yet -- is the one it cannot express here. Superseded decisions are listed like any other; the identifier that supersedes them comes back but nothing filters on it.

The typed maintenance.decision_log_list_scoped operation lists decisions by subject and status. Each filter is dropped when empty, so sending neither lists every decision -- which is also what maintenance.decision_log_list does with an empty outcome, by a different route. This one breaks ties on the identifier where that one does not, so its order is stable and that one's is not when two decisions share a creation stamp.

The typed maintenance.mark_revisit_due operation replaces the sweep that flags active decisions whose review date has arrived. The two states, the requirement that a decision carry a review date at all, and the database clock are fixed policy, as they are for the two sweeps beside it. Unlike those, this backend separates a failed statement from an empty sweep, so the boundary can report the failure instead of an untouched log.

The typed learning.decision_log_set_outcome operation replaces the outcome write. The text is stored as given -- nothing checks it against a vocabulary -- and an identifier naming no decision updates nothing and is acknowledged just the same, so the reply says the statement ran rather than that it changed anything. An empty outcome is allowed, which is how a decision whose outcome is not yet known is recorded.

The typed learning.decision_log_set_revisit operation replaces the revisit write. The stamp is the caller's and is stored as text without being parsed, so an unparseable one is accepted here and fails at whatever compares it later -- which is worth recording because the sweep that acts on revisit stamps compares them as text. An empty stamp clears the revisit.

The typed learning.decision_log_set_status operation replaces the status write. Like the outcome beside it the value is stored unchecked, so a caller can put a decision into a status no reader understands. Unlike the outcome an empty status is refused, because a decision always has one and the empty string is not it.

The typed lifecycle.dimension_reset operation keeps schema replacement, maintenance marking, and requeue accounting inside one DB2-owned operator transaction while returning only bounded structured evidence.

The typed maintenance.directive_list operation lists epistemic directives by state and cause. Each filter is dropped when empty rather than matched against the empty string, so sending neither lists every directive -- four different statements behind one name. The order is by priority, then newest, then identifier, so it is stable but a caller paging by limit alone re-reads the same head.

The typed maintenance.directive_by_entity operation finds the open directives anchored to an entity. The comparison lowers the stored anchor and not the argument, so a caller that sends a name as written matches nothing -- the field is named for what it expects. Only open directives match, so a resolved one is invisible here whatever its anchor.

The typed maintenance.directive_by_file operation finds the open directives anchored to a file. The path is compared exactly, where the entity matcher beside it compares a lowered anchor, so the two differ in a way neither name nor reply shows. Only open directives match.

The typed maintenance.directive_by_lexical operation finds the open directives whose question or topic contains any of a clause's words. The clause is not SQL: the backend takes alphanumeric runs from it, lowercases them, drops anything under two characters and the literal word OR, keeps at most sixteen, and matches each as a substring. So punctuation and quoting are ignored, and a seventeenth word is silently not searched for.

The typed maintenance.directive_record_surface operation counts a surfacing of an open directive and stamps when it happened. Like the suppression beside it the state guard lives in the statement, and a directive that was not open is indistinguishable from a failed write in what the backend returns.

The typed maintenance.directive_resolve operation replaces the resolution write. Only an open directive is touched, so resolving one twice does nothing the second time. The resolving memory is stored without being checked to exist -- there is no foreign key here -- so a caller can point a resolved directive at a memory that was never created, and nothing will notice until something tries to read it.

The typed maintenance.directive_suppress operation closes an open epistemic directive. The statement carries its own state = 'open' guard, so deciding and writing are one action. A directive that was not open is reported exactly as a failed statement is, because the backend returns the same value for both; the catalog records that collapse rather than leaving a caller to discover that failed sometimes means already suppressed.

The typed maintenance.directive_sweep_expired operation replaces the sweep that closes epistemic directives whose validity window has passed. It carries the same fixed policy as the prospective sweep it sits beside: the two states, the requirement that a directive carry a window at all, and the database clock. A directive is an instruction the system holds itself to, so retiring one early on a caller's wrong clock would quietly drop a constraint that is still in force.
The typed lifecycle.embedder_serving_id operation replaces the curator replay direct caller with DB2's bounded effective vector-space identity; empty remains the legacy no-identity state.
The typed lifecycle.embedding_dimension operation replaces production direct callers; the effective pgvector schema width remains DB2 authority.
The typed lifecycle.embedding_refusals operation replaces the KB health direct caller; the rejected width is DB2 pgvector diagnostic evidence.
The typed lifecycle.embedding_refusals operation replaces the KB health direct caller; refusal count is DB2 pgvector diagnostic evidence.

The typed custody.enrollment_active operation replaces the enrollment probe. A revoked enrollment reads as inactive, exactly like one that was never enrolled, so a caller cannot tell the two apart through this operation -- which matters because they mean different things to whoever is deciding what to do next.

The typed index.entity_observation_count operation replaces the observation count. It counts distinct memories rather than observation rows and matches the entity case-insensitively, so a memory naming an entity twice counts once and a differently cased spelling still matches. Neither is visible in a bare number, so both are policy.

The typed index.entity_edge_bump_utility operation adjusts the utility of every edge touching an entity -- at either end, by the same amount, in one statement, with no bound on how many rows that is. Each result is clamped into the range the column keeps, so a delta past it moves an edge to the limit rather than being refused, and repeating the call stops changing anything once every edge is pinned. The reply says the statement ran and never how many edges moved.

The typed index.entity_edges_for_entity operation lists the edges touching an entity, with the identifier and endpoints of each. Both directions are unioned without an ORDER BY, so when the limit bites, which edges come back is whatever the database returned first. Semantic edges are excluded, and the endpoints are matched exactly rather than case-insensitively.

The typed index.entity_neighbors operation lists an entity's graph neighbours. Edges are followed in both directions and the two halves are unioned without an ORDER BY, so when the limit bites, which neighbours come back is whatever the database returned first. Semantic edges are excluded. The weight column is a BIGINT and the row narrows it to a 32-bit number, so a weight past that range is already truncated before it reaches this boundary.

The typed index.entity_neighbors_filtered operation lists an entity's neighbours through one or two named relations. An empty second relation narrows the query to the first rather than being an error. A limit of zero is quietly replaced with twenty, so a caller asking for no limit gets one. The weight ordering is optional and off by default, and without it the limit keeps whichever rows came back first, which is not the strongest ones.

The typed index.entity_neighbors_weighted operation lists an entity's neighbours with both the utility stored on each edge and the utility after decay. The two differ by how long ago the edge was last touched, so a caller comparing them is comparing a value to its own age. Both are signed and clamped to the range the column keeps. As with the plain neighbour listing, edges are followed in both directions and nothing orders the result, so which neighbours survive the limit is arbitrary.

The typed index.entity_edge_normalize_weights operation replaces the per-relation weight rescale. The statement already skips rows that would be rewritten to the value they hold, so a converged graph reports zero rather than rewriting every edge, and the scale stays fixed policy behind the handler.

The typed index.entity_outbound_neighbors operation lists the entities an entity points at. It differs from index.entity_neighbors in exactly one way that the identical reply cannot show: this one follows edges leaving the entity and that one follows edges in both directions. A caller that wants the graph treated as undirected and reaches for this name gets half the answer and no indication of it.

The typed index.entity_edge_prune_orphans operation replaces the maintenance pass that drops entity edges no surviving memory references. The tiers that count as a reference are fixed policy behind the handler, so a caller cannot widen or narrow what counts as orphaned.

The typed index.entity_edges_by_token operation finds the edges where a token is either endpoint or the relation itself. That third comparison is what separates it from index.entity_edges_for_entity beside it: a token naming a relation matches every edge of that kind. The comparison is case-insensitive, unlike that operation's, and the heaviest edges come first.

The typed index.entity_top_triples operation lists the heaviest distinct source-relation-target triples across the whole graph. The identifier is selected as a literal zero, because a distinct triple may stand for several edges -- so unlike every other edge listing, no row here names an edge a caller could read back. The row shape is shared with those listings, which is the only reason the field is present at all.

The typed index.entity_top_partners operation ranks the entities most connected to one entity through a relation. Unlike the neighbour listings beside it the endpoint is matched case-insensitively, so two spellings of a name are one entity here and two entities there. Both directions are summed per partner, so the weight is a total rather than any single edge's, and it can exceed what a single edge's weight column could hold.

The typed index.entity_top_targets operation ranks the entities one entity points at through a relation. It is index.entity_top_partners with one direction instead of two, and the reply is identical, so the names are the only thing distinguishing a directed ranking from an undirected one. Like its partner it matches the endpoint case-insensitively, unlike the plain neighbour listings which do not.

The typed index.entity_walk_step_typed operation returns the edges touching a node, heaviest first, at most fifty. The node may be either end, so the reply's source and target say which way each edge points rather than repeating the argument. An edge with no recorded relation identifier or endpoint kind reads back as the co-discussed relation and the other kind, so a default and a real value are indistinguishable in the reply.

Builds an entity key from a project and path entirely in memory. It must not become a call: keys are compared, so a caller and DB2 that disagree about the format do not fail, they silently stop matching. The format is shared vocabulary and belongs in one definition both sides compile against.

The symbol counterpart of the file key builder, and private for the same reason. Both encode their components the same way and both must stay that way; a divergence produces keys that look valid and match nothing.

The typed index.entity_profile_card operation replaces the card read. The entity is matched case-insensitively, and the card crosses as whatever JSON DB2 has stored: this boundary bounds its length and refuses an embedded NUL, and does not parse it. A caller receiving malformed JSON is receiving what was written, which is the honest behaviour but not an obvious one.

The typed index.entity_profile_fresh operation replaces the freshness probe. The window is a Postgres interval the caller supplies and DB2 evaluates against its own clock, so an unparseable interval makes the statement fail rather than answer false; the wire bounds its length but cannot check its syntax.
The typed learning.evidence_enqueue operation replaces the evidence queue insert. Enqueuing something already queued does nothing and is acknowledged, so a caller cannot tell a new job from a repeat.

The typed learning.evidence_mark_failed operation replaces the failure write. The attempt counter is incremented by the statement rather than supplied, so a caller can record that something failed but neither set the count nor read it back. An empty error text is allowed, which is how a failure with nothing to say is recorded.

The typed maintenance.evidence_reembed_all operation replaces the reset that requeues every evidence index row after an embedder version change. Its reach is total and deliberately so: it takes no predicate, resets the attempt count and discards the last error on every row. Recording that as fixed policy is the point of the entry -- the reach cannot be narrowed or widened by a caller, and the discarded failure history is stated rather than left to be discovered by someone wondering where the errors went.

The typed learning.failed_query_bump operation replaces the failure tally. It is two statements with no transaction around them -- an upsert and then a read -- so the count it answers with can include a bump another caller made in between. That is the backend's behaviour and is on the record because a single number cannot show it.

The typed learning.fidelity_attribution_count operation replaces the attribution count. Which artifact kind counts as a fidelity attribution is DB2 policy fixed in the statement, so a caller cannot ask for a different kind through this operation.
The typed lifecycle.health operation replaces production direct callers; PostgreSQL schema and extension readiness remain DB2 authority.
Database opening, schema application, and pool construction are private process bootstrap; the supervisor starts DB2 before exposing any bus capability.
The typed lifecycle.health operation proves the DB2 owner is initialized before reporting PostgreSQL and canonical KB readiness.

The typed maintenance.async_pending_count operation replaces the queue-depth read. It counts only jobs still pending, so a job already being worked on is not in the answer -- a caller using this as a backlog gauge is measuring what has not started rather than what is outstanding.

The typed organization.blob_referenced operation replaces the reference probe. It answers whether any document asset still points at the blob, not how many do: the statement stops at the first row, which is what makes it cheap enough to run before a delete.

The typed organization.doc_assets_delete_for_doc operation deletes the assets extracted from one document. The statement narrows twice more than the arguments suggest: the generation must be the project's current one, and the document must be of kind pdf. So naming a real document of any other kind deletes nothing and reports zero, which is also what an already-clean document reports.
The typed organization.doc_delete operation removes a document row by identifier, reporting an error when nothing matched.

The typed organization.doc_exists_by_hash operation replaces the content probe. The hash is matched exactly and within one scope, so the same content in another scope does not count -- which is what makes this usable as a per-scope duplicate check rather than a global one.

The typed organization.document_stored_hash operation reads the hash recorded for a document. Only the project's current generation answers, so a document indexed under an older generation reads back empty -- the same empty as a path nobody has indexed, and the same as a failed read. A caller using this to decide whether a file changed sees an unchanged file as a new one across a generation bump.

The typed organization.document_hash_exists operation asks whether a project's current generation already holds content with this hash. Two tables are searched and one path comes back, so the sample names one file with that content and never says how many there are, nor which of the two tables it came from. Both halves are scoped to the current generation, so identical content indexed under an older one does not count as present.

The typed organization.document_chunk_ids operation lists the chunks a file was split into. Only the project's current generation is listed, so a file indexed under an older one has no chunks as far as this operation is concerned. The list stops at the row bound and says nothing about having stopped, which matters because its caller, the curator invalidation, uses the list to decide what to stale -- a file with more chunks than the bound leaves the rest valid.

The typed index.file_index_delete_current_generation operation deletes a project's file index for its current generation only. It is one letter away from index.file_index_delete_project, which deletes every generation, and the names are the only thing telling them apart. The project name goes through a helper called db2_kb_resolve_project which copies it and resolves nothing, so an alias matches no rows. A project with no current generation reports zero, and so does an index that was already empty.

The typed index.file_index_delete_project operation removes a project's file index entries across every generation. The name goes through db2_kb_resolve_project, which despite the name copies the string and does nothing else, so the project is matched exactly and an alias matches nothing. Unlike the document clears it is a single statement with nothing to leave half-done, and it does not check whether that statement finished, so a failure reports zero deleted rather than an error.
The typed lifecycle.health operation exposes canonical KB-table readiness together with the schema probe; that evidence remains DB2 authority.

The typed maintenance.ingest_queue_fail operation replaces the failure write. The completion stamp is DB2's clock, and the statement has no condition on the job's current state, so a job that already succeeded is moved to failed just the same. The backend discards the step result, so the acknowledgement means the statement was prepared and nothing more: a job identifier that matches nothing is acknowledged.

The typed maintenance.ingest_queue_reset_running operation replaces the startup recovery that returns queue rows abandoned by a dead worker to the pending pool. The two states and the clearing of started_at are fixed policy. Clearing the claim instant is the part that matters: a row left marked as claimed by a process that no longer exists is work that never runs again, and a caller able to skip the clear would hand back a row that still looks taken.

The typed organization.pdf_quarantine_confirm operation replaces the confirm. It only touches a pending PDF at the project's current generation, so a stale one, or one already confirmed, counts zero rather than failing -- a caller reading zero as an error would be wrong.

The typed organization.pdf_quarantine_reject operation replaces the reject. It is the mirror of confirm and deletes rather than clears, under the same generation and pending conditions; the count is rows removed.

The typed organization.pdf_tsr_state operation reads a PDF's text-scan state. The statement narrows three ways the arguments do not show: the document must be a PDF, it must be in the project's current generation, and it must not still be awaiting a quarantine decision. A document held in pending quarantine therefore reads back empty, which is also what a document of another kind reads back, and what a missing one reads back.

The typed organization.fence_active operation replaces the fence probe. It composes two runtime-state reads and fails closed: an identity row with no heartbeat reads as active, so a partially written fence is never reported inactive. That rule is the whole point of the probe and is not visible in the Boolean it answers with.

The typed organization.purge_fence_clear operation removes a purge fence. It checks the fence still names this generation and purge before deleting, inside the transaction it holds, so a caller cannot clear someone else's fence. The two rows go in the order identity then timestamp, which is the reverse of how they are written: an interrupted clear leaves an orphan timestamp, which the fence check treats as no fence, so the failure direction is open rather than stuck.

The typed organization.purge_fence_heartbeat operation refreshes a purge fence's timestamp. Unlike the bare advisory guard it uses, this operation opens the transaction, takes the lock, checks the fence still names this generation and purge, writes and commits -- all inside the module -- so it is one of the few purge-route pieces that crosses the boundary intact. A fence naming a different purge is refused, and so is one that has been cleared; the reply cannot tell those from a database error.

The typed organization.release_add_doc operation replaces the release membership insert. Both ends are foreign keys, so an unknown release or an unknown document is refused and the reply says so -- this is not a write that always succeeds. Adding a document already in the release does nothing and is still acknowledged, so a caller cannot tell a repeat from a first add, which is what makes a retry safe.

The typed organization.release_create operation opens a document release. The name is unique, so a second create with a name already taken is refused and answers zero -- the same zero as any other failure, and the operation gives no way to ask for the identifier the existing release has. Identifiers start at one, so zero never names a release. It pairs with organization.release_add_doc, which takes the identifier this returns.

The typed custody.release_get_active operation reads the pointer to the release the system currently answers as. Zero covers three different situations: no key, a value that does not parse, and a value that is not positive. The parse happens through atoll, which returns zero for garbage without saying so, and the catalog records both collapses rather than letting a zero read as a confident no release.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_get operation replaces the runtime-state read, and is the first on the described wire format: its request and reply are a schema in the catalog rather than a shape someone wrote codecs for. A key that is not set reads back as the empty value, so a caller cannot tell an unset key from one set to nothing -- which matters because runtime_state_touch writes a stamp and reading nothing back looks the same as never having touched it.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_set operation replaces the runtime-state write. Unlike runtime_state_touch beside it, the value is the caller's rather than DB2's clock, and an existing key is overwritten rather than refused -- this sets, it does not create.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_touch operation replaces the timestamp upsert. The value written is DB2's clock rather than anything the caller supplies, so this records that something happened and never when a caller says it did.

The typed custody.vector_rebuild_lock_release operation deletes the rebuild lock row. It does not check who holds it, so any caller can release another's lock; that is recorded rather than implied. It returns void, so like the proposal archive it cannot report a failure and the catalog says so.

The typed custody.vector_rebuild_lock_try_acquire operation claims the vector rebuild lock. It is a check followed by a separate write, so two callers can both observe the lock free and both claim it: it does not provide mutual exclusion. The catalog records that as atomicity check-then-set and mutually_exclusive false so the gap is stated where a reader will find it, rather than inferred from the word lock.

Per-kind promotion, demotion, and expiry thresholds are a private input to the tier-cycle operations that apply them; exposing the lookup alone would let a caller act on thresholds DB2 had already superseded.

The typed learning.commits_in_last_7_days operation replaces the recent-commit count. The seven-day window and the clock it is measured against are both DB2's and never cross, so a caller cannot widen the window or supply its own now; the count is only meaningful beside that fact.

The typed learning.proposal_bump_corroboration operation replaces the corroboration bump. Only a pending proposal is bumped, but the acknowledgement reports that the statement ran and not that a row matched, so corroborating a committed proposal -- or one that does not exist -- does nothing and says it succeeded.

The typed learning.proposal_mark_committed operation replaces the commit write. The typed learning.proposals_archive_expired operation replaces the sweep that archives learning proposals past their expiry. The states, the archive reason and the database clock are fixed policy. This backend returns void and logs its failures, so the boundary cannot report one either; the catalog records reports_failure as false rather than letting an always-ok acknowledgement imply a guarantee that is not there.
Lease scope terminates process-local PostgreSQL ownership and has no wire representation; it disappears when the enclosing DB2 work becomes one bounded request.
Idle-lease release is process-local pool hygiene, not a remote database operation; the standalone owner releases its own leases between complete bus requests.

Clearing a process-local maintenance job binding has no wire representation; explicit request scope replaces the caller-owned thread-local lifetime.
Beginning a PostgreSQL transaction from thread-local maintenance state is private DB2 execution; a typed operation validates explicit scope and begins its own transaction instead.
A caller-controlled commit is forbidden across the module boundary; each declared maintenance mutation commits before publishing its bounded reply.
A caller-controlled rollback is process-local transaction cleanup; failed or cancelled maintenance operations roll back inside DB2 before returning transport status.

The typed memory.aggregate operation replaces the aggregation read. Identifiers cross; it is unscoped.

The typed memory.briefing_active_entities operation ranks the entities mentioned by recently touched memories. The typed memory.get operation replaces the row read. A null provenance category reads back as user_stated.

The typed memory.get_by_unit_id operation resolves a unit to its memory and shares memory.get's row format. It does not fill the same row: its statement asks for eleven columns, so salience, provenance_category and use_cases come back empty rather than absent, and a caller cannot tell an unread column from a genuinely empty one. That is why each operation's policy lists the columns it actually reads. It conflates an absent row with a failed statement the same way memory.get does.

The typed memory.get_content operation replaces the canonical text read and is the companion to memory.update_content. A missing memory is reported as not_found rather than as empty content, because a stored row may legitimately hold an empty string and the two answers are different.

The backend succeeds only for a non-empty session and reports an absent memory and a blank column identically, so the wire reply is non-empty on ok and everything else is not_found rather than inventing a distinction the backend cannot make.

The typed memory.has_workspace_tag operation replaces the existence probe over workspace attribution rows, preserving its hit-or-miss result; the join stays DB2 authority and no workspace identity crosses the bus.

The typed memory.has_scope_type operation replaces the existence probe over scope attribution rows, preserving its hit-or-miss result; the caller names the scope kind and learns only whether one exists, never which scope value.

The typed memory.health_retention operation runs contradiction pruning together with health-snapshot pruning under one fixed policy, so this half is never invoked on its own.
The typed memory.health_counters operation returns the complete rolling-window aggregate under the fixed host promotion policy; DB2 owns every count and the host derives only ratios from them.
The typed memory.health_record operation carries only the three host-observed cycle counters; DB2 owns the corpus total and the fixed one-day conflict window it inserts alongside them.
The typed memory.effectiveness_update operation preserves the host-computed binary64 value while DB2 owns the canonical effectiveness column update.
The typed memory.key_exists operation replaces the bounded exact-key probe while preserving explicit backend-error handling; canonical memory keys remain DB2 authority.
The typed memory.key_exists_in_tier_pair operation replaces the bounded canonical-key and tier-pair probe while preserving its Boolean hit-or-miss result.

The typed memory.lifecycle_sweep_expired operation replaces the pending time-to-live archival pass; the source state, target state, and archive reason stay fixed policy behind the handler so no caller can archive a different set of rows.
The typed memory.link_delete operation replaces the single relation delete; the link identity is the caller's only input and the relation graph stays DB2 authority.

The typed memory.list_rows operation replaces the tier and kind listing. It is the only read here whose statement is assembled: the tier and kind clauses appear only when their value is non-empty, so an empty value is no filter on that column rather than a match against the empty string, and this is four statements sharing one name. Its LIMIT was interpolated from an unbounded caller integer and is a bounded field on the wire. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the other scoped reads.

The typed maintenance.retryable_index_failures operation lists the memories whose indexing failed and is still worth retrying. Oldest failure first, so a caller working through the list makes progress rather than retrying the same head. A limit of zero adds no LIMIT clause, leaving the row bound as the only stop. Distinct memory identifiers come back, so a memory that failed several times appears once and the reply says nothing about how many attempts it has left.

The typed memory.list_session_scope_priority operation replaces the row reader. Two decisions are on the record with it. The ordering is DB2's, computed against DB2's own scope tables, so it stays behind the handler. And the scope the ordering depends on now travels in the request: the backend reads it from a thread-local that db2_memory_scope_context_set writes, which does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.list_session_scope_priority_like operation replaces the filtered variant of the priority list. The term is bound as a SQL LIKE pattern rather than a literal, so a wildcard the caller writes is significant and a caller sending a literal percent sign gets a wider result than it asked for -- that is on the record because the wire cannot show it. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the unfiltered variant.

The typed memory.load_eval_corpus operation replaces the corpus loader. It tries three plans in order and the first to return a row wins, so the reply carries the label of the plan that answered: which corpus a caller got is not recoverable from the identifiers. Each plan carries its own LIMIT of 100, so the request limit bounds what is read back rather than what the plan selects. Identifiers cross; it is unscoped.

The typed memory.negation_fts_search operation replaces the negation search. The tokens cross; joining them with OR and building the tsquery is the handler's, and so is the 1600-byte bound on the joined query, which truncates silently once the tokens exceed it. websearch_to_tsquery is used precisely because it does not syntax-error on arbitrary input. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the other scoped searches.

The typed memory.negation_tokens_update operation replaces the extracted-token write, bounded to the extractor's own output width. The backend maps a null to an empty string and stores it, so an empty value is a request that clears the column rather than a malformed one.

The typed memory.pick_first_temporal_ref operation replaces the highest-ranked temporal reference lookup. The ordering is fixed policy inside the statement rather than a caller input, and a memory with no usable reference is reported as not_found since the backend succeeds only for a non-empty key.
The typed memory.expire operation wipes the L0 rows together with their provenance, so this half never runs alone and no partially expired L0 state is observable across the bus.
The typed memory.expire operation clears L0 provenance immediately before the rows it describes, inside one DB2 action that owns both halves.
The typed memory.expire operation applies each kind's own idle window from the private lifecycle thresholds, so the stale-L1 delete is never reachable with a caller-chosen kind or window.
The typed memory.expire operation clears stale-L1 provenance immediately before the rows it describes, under the same per-kind window and inside the same DB2 action.

The typed memory.demote operation cascades reduced confidence to dependants of the rows it just demoted, matched by the stamp it issued; exposing the cascade alone would let a caller match rows a different action had stamped.

The typed memory.match_error_keys operation finds the memories whose key appears in an error message. The comparison puts the key on the pattern side of a LIKE, so a key containing a percent or an underscore is a wildcard: one such key matches text it has nothing to do with, and nothing escapes it. The scan reads every L1 and L2 memory above the confidence floor, so cost grows with the corpus, and the caller sees a truncated list and a full one the same way.

The typed memory.promote_stable operation applies the complete fixed stability policy — tier, kinds, confidence floor, use count, and settling window — so callers cannot promote rows into the slow-changing tier on terms of their own.

The typed memory.reclassify_directives operation fixes the tiers and directive kinds and carries only the approval gate, which is a genuine caller choice: the batch path runs ungated while the operator approval path requires a recorded approval for policies.

Provenance cleanup is an internal compatibility step of the complete memory.delete operation; it must commit with canonical row, vector, relation, and derived-state deletion rather than cross the bus independently.
Provenance append is private bookkeeping inside complete insert, merge, consolidate, and supersede operations; no generic caller-controlled provenance mutation crosses the bus.

The typed memory.prune_orphaned_l0 operation replaces the doctor-invoked retention delete for expired unlinked short-term rows; the tier and age window stay fixed policy behind the handler so no caller can widen the delete.

The typed memory.relations_for_entity operation lists the relations an entity takes part in. Either end matches, and both are compared case-insensitively, so the reply's own source and target say which way each relation points rather than repeating the argument. The order is newest memory first, then heaviest, so the limit keeps the most recent rather than the strongest.

The typed memory.relations_search operation searches relations by substring across both endpoints, the relation name and the fact text. The query is wrapped in wildcards rather than matched as one, so a short query matches almost every row and the limit decides what a caller sees. Nothing escapes the query, so a percent or underscore in it widens the match further.

The typed memory.relations_search_as_of operation searches relations as they stood at an instant. A relation with an empty start stamp counts as valid before the instant and one with an empty end stamp as valid after it, so a relation with neither is returned for every instant -- absence reads as always rather than never. The stamps are compared as text, so a differently formatted instant compares wrongly rather than failing.

The typed memory.relations_supporting operation finds the relations that carry a stated fact about an entity. It differs from memory.relations_for_entity twice over: the token matches either endpoint as a substring rather than exactly, and a relation whose fact text is empty is skipped, because a relation with nothing written on it supports nothing.
The raw row insert is private implementation of a complete memory.insert operation, which must validate input, insert the canonical row, attach provenance and scope, and commit before replying.

The typed memory.scene_member_exists operation replaces the membership probe. A statement that cannot run answers false, indistinguishable from an absent membership.

Per-candidate rank probes would expose chatty implicit state; DB2 applies scope ranking inside the complete bounded memory search and returns only the ranked result set.
A setter for thread-local workspace and project scope cannot cross a process boundary; typed memory requests carry the bounded scope with the operation that consumes it.

It returns identifiers rather than rows, because the generated client sizes its reply buffer as a local array and sixty-four memory rows do not belong on a caller's stack; the caller reattaches content through memory.get_content. The session scope travels in the request for the same reason as list_session_scope_priority.

The typed memory.touch operation replaces the retrieval-accounting bump; the increment and the stamp are fixed policy behind the handler so a caller can record that a memory was used but cannot choose by how much or when.

The typed memory.unit_edge_exists operation replaces the edge probe. Both orders are tried, so an edge stored either way answers true and the arguments are interchangeable -- the opposite of memory.scene_member_exists beside it, and not visible in a Boolean. The edge type is ignored, and nothing stops the same pair being stored twice, so this answers whether the units are connected at all and never how.

Private second half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

Private first half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

The typed memory.unit_ids_for_memory operation lists the units a memory was split into. The statement has no ORDER BY, so the order is whatever Postgres returns and is not stable between calls -- anything pairing this list with another by position is relying on something nobody promised. A memory that does not exist and one with no units both answer with nothing.
